name: Aisha Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Aisha, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Lindqvist and Sons, a family-owned farm supply wholesaler. We sell feed, seed, fencing, fertiliser and tools to about 80 farm shops across three counties. I start at 7 with a coffee and the order book, and I ring the mills about feed prices, because grain moves with the weather. In spring it's seed and fertiliser, in autumn it's winter feed and fencing. I've worked with the same suppliers for sixteen years, and some of them came to my wedding. What wears me out is the seasons: when the rain won't stop, everyone wants everything at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds right to me. I've heard these promises before and the farm shops still ring me on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say there's nothing to worry about, and let's get on with the season. At church or with friends I'd say I'm not fussed. I've never used these AI things and nothing I've seen makes me want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel steady, but not carefree. Old Mr. Lindqvist is nearly seventy and his son hasn't shown much interest in the business. If it sold to a bigger group, buying would be done from a head office. That worry has been with me for years. And we've got only about three months saved with the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as usual. I'd keep my relationships with the mills and the farm shops warm, and I'd try to keep savings climbing. I'd maybe ask the owner what his plans are, because I don't like not knowing. I'd also keep my community role at church, since that's my second family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. Some low worry about the firm's future, but nothing new from this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm might be sold. How would that affect your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bigger group would put in their own buying system and their own people. I'd be told it's more efficient. I've seen a rival firm do that, and the buyer there, a woman I know, was moved to a customer service desk. She said the new system didn't know the farmers. But the system won.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI really is mostly hype, as in this picture, does that protect you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If the software turns out to be rubbish, a customer will still want to ring someone who knows their name and knows what their sheep need. But it won't protect me from a buyer who decides to cut costs, which happens with or without AI.

say: I'd say there's **nothing to worry about** and we should get on with the season.
I'd add that I've **never used** these AI tools and don't want to.
think: I feel steady, but the owner is nearly seventy and a **sale** worries me.
A bigger group would **buy from head office**.
do: Keep my relationships with the **mills and farm shops** warm.
Ask the owner what his **plans** are, because I dislike not knowing.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a low worry about the firm's future.
S0.quote: If the software turns out to be rubbish, a customer will still want to ring someone who knows their name and knows what their sheep need.
fieldNote: Her fear is **ownership change**, not the technology, and she has a real example.
She's **proud** of never using AI, which reads as part of her identity.
Church and community sit beside work as a **second safety net**.

steps.text: Keep ringing the mills and farm shops every week as usual
Ask Mr. Lindqvist what he plans for the firm
Add a fixed amount each month to the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's closer. Buying and checking and answering customers is exactly what my office does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should be careful, and I'd ask what a machine really knows about a farmer's land. With friends I'd say jobs like mine will shrink and we'd better look after each other. I'd also say work and family come first, whatever technology comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the owners will use any excuse to cut. My team of four may become two. The order-taking that Gunnar and Marie do would go to a system first, and that bothers me, because they're good people with children. I'd be asked to manage the change, and I don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to learn something about it, and I'd hate that. I'd ask Marie, who's more at ease with computers, to show me one thing at a time on Friday afternoons. I'd cut our spending by about a tenth, build the savings, and speak with Henrik about whether his carpentry could take on more work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then more worried when I think about Gunnar and Marie. Some anger, too. Nobody asked us whether we wanted this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody asked you. Who would you like to have asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people deciding. Owners, investors, the people who build the software. They sit in offices and talk about efficiency while a family has to explain a drop in income to the kids. I'm not against progress, but progress that only helps people at the top isn't progress to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you hate the idea of learning the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like I'd be helping to remove my friends. I don't want to be the one who teaches the machine to do Gunnar's job, because Gunnar has four children and a church to feed on Sundays. But I can see that if I refuse, I'm out too.

say: I'd say we should be careful and ask what a machine knows about a **farmer's land**.
I'd say we should **look after each other**.
think: I think the owners will use any excuse to **cut**, and four might become two.
Order-taking by **Gunnar and Marie** goes first, which bothers me.
do: Ask Marie to show me **one tool** at a time on Friday afternoons.
Cut spending by a **tenth** and build savings.
Ask Henrik whether his **carpentry** could take on more work.
feel: **Uneasy**, then angry that nobody asked us.
S1.quote: I don't want to be the one who teaches the machine to do Gunnar's job, because Gunnar has four children and a church to feed on Sundays.
fieldNote: Her reluctance is **moral**: she doesn't want to be the one who teaches the tool.
She blames **owners and investors** more than the technology.
Her faith and community show up as **loyalty to colleagues**.

steps.text: Ask Marie to teach me one tool each Friday afternoon
Cut family spending by about a tenth
Ask Henrik to take on more carpentry jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's no time at all. My children would barely be through a school year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to stand up for ordinary working families before this happens. I'd say it at church, at work, wherever I could. I'd say this must not be allowed to wreck communities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is gone. Buying is thinking work, and if a machine does thinking cheaper, the firm doesn't need a senior buyer. Henrik's carpentry is hands-on, so it's safer, but a carpenter's income here is up and down. If both our incomes sagged, we'd be in real trouble, and I think that's likely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to cutting: no holiday, a cheaper car, everything pared back. I'd talk to our pastor and my parents about what help we could count on. I'd start looking at jobs that are hands-on: a farm shop manager, or a role in a seed company's field team. And I'd vote for whoever promised to protect families like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry. I'd pray about it a lot, and I'd still lie awake working out how we pay for school clothes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd turn to the church and your parents. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents live forty minutes away and have a spare room. If it came to it we could move in for a while, rent the house out, and keep the mortgage going. Pride would hurt, but family is family. The church would bring meals and help with the children, because that's what we do for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you most want your children to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're okay as long as we're together. I'd tell my children that the house and the job are things, and that what matters is the family sitting round the same table. I'd mean it, even while I was scared.

say: I'd say governments must **stand up** for ordinary working families first.
I'd say this must not **wreck communities**.
think: I think my job is **gone**; buying is thinking work a machine does cheaper.
Henrik's **carpentry** is hands-on, but income here swings up and down.
do: Cut hard: no holiday, a **cheaper car**, everything pared back.
Talk to our **pastor** and my parents about what help we could count on.
Look at **hands-on roles** like farm shop manager or a seed company field team.
feel: **Frightened** and angry, praying and lying awake over school clothes.
S2.quote: I'd tell my children that the house and the job are things, and that what matters is the family sitting round the same table.
fieldNote: She reaches for **family and church** first, then politics, a traditional pattern.
She reads the **robot gap** well: hands-on field roles buy time.
Expected **lost pay** and a thin cushion make this clearly alarmed.

steps.text: Cut spending hard and trade down to a cheaper car
Ask my parents about staying with them if the house is rented out
Apply for farm shop manager and seed company field roles
Vote for and campaign for family support policies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I could just about see my way through that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for families and employers to prepare if they get started. I'd ask the owner to be honest with us, and I'd talk with other families from church about what we'd all do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd keep my job for three years and then it starts to go. My children would be 17 and 14, and that's the expensive stretch. I'd feel like the clock was ticking over the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in farm business management at the agricultural college, which suits my knowledge of farmers. I'd cut spending a little and save more, aiming at six months. I'd also ask the owner whether the firm could move me to an area where I deal in person, like sales visits to farm shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a purpose. A date and a plan are easier than a vague fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why farm business management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know what farmers worry about: feed prices, weather, the bank. I could advise them directly, which machines can't do as well, because farmers want someone who's stood in a muddy yard. A farmer will trust a woman who's stood in his muddy yard more than a program on a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you manage the course with the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Evenings, after supper, with Henrik minding the children. It would be hard. I'd also lean on my mother for school pick-ups two days a week. It takes a family, and I'm lucky to have one that'd pitch in.

say: I'd say **five years** is long enough if families and employers start.
I'd talk with **other families** from church about what we'd all do.
think: I think I'd keep my job for **three years**, then it starts to go.
My children at 17 and 14 would be the **expensive stretch**.
do: Start a part-time **farm business** course at the agricultural college.
Save toward **six months** and cut spending a little.
Ask the owner for a role with **in-person** sales visits.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a purpose, since a plan beats a vague fear.
S3.quote: A farmer will trust a woman who's stood in his muddy yard more than a program on a phone.
fieldNote: She builds on **trust with farmers**, a human advantage she values.
Her plan depends on **family help** from Henrik and her mother.
Resistance to AI stays; her move is toward **in-person work**.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time farm business course at the agricultural college
Ask Mr. Lindqvist to move me into in-person sales visits
Save toward six months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then Ingrid is 22 and Jonas 19. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the main thing is to keep working, keep family close, and keep faith. I'd push my church and community groups to talk about helping each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel mostly safe. Plenty can happen in ten years, and maybe the people in charge will do something sensible. But I'd also know myself: I'd put off learning, because I don't like new tools. That's my weak point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save steadily, aim for six months, and pay down the mortgage. I'd learn the basics of the tools slowly, probably once the children are older. I'd keep building relationships with farmers, and I'd think about a role in farm advice or supply in the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with some unease about putting things off. It's a long time, and long times can be wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put things off. What would help you not to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone to nudge me. Marie, probably, or Henrik. I need a reason that matters: my children, a deadline. I only move when something is pressing on the table, which is why ten years is a danger for someone like me. I'm honest about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your children about work in ten years' time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn a trade or a craft and be useful to people. A person who can fix, grow, build or care for something will always be needed. I'd also tell them to marry kindly and keep a savings account. Those are my old-fashioned rules, and I'd still give them.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long, and we should keep working and keep family close.
I'd push my church to talk about **helping each other**.
think: I feel mostly safe, but I'd **put off** learning because I dislike new tools.
The people in charge might do something **sensible**.
do: Save steadily toward **six months** and pay down the mortgage.
Learn the tools' **basics** slowly, once the children are older.
Build relationships with farmers for a future **advice** role.
S4.quote: I only move when something is pressing on the table, which is why ten years is a danger for someone like me.
fieldNote: Her weak point is **procrastination**, which she names herself.
Her advice to her children centres on **trades and being useful**.
Ten years eases her mood, but her **resistance** is what she worries about.

steps.text: Put away a fixed sum monthly until six months are saved
Learn the basics of one buying tool with Marie's help
Build contacts for a future farm advice role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My children are small, our savings are thin, and I don't learn new things quickly. What would help is a firm that speaks honestly, support for families while we retrain, and my church and family nearby.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that not everyone can just learn the tools and carry on. Some of us built our jobs on knowing farmers' names, and I don't know where that goes when the order book is a machine.

headlineQuote: Some of us built our jobs on knowing farmers' names, and I don't know where that goes when the order book is a machine.
portrait: Aisha Olsen, 43, is **senior buyer** at a family-owned farm supply wholesaler, with a carpenter husband and two school-age children.
Traditional and **resistant**: never uses AI, and she sees refusing as loyalty to her colleagues.
About **three months** saved and a mortgage; her biggest steady worry is the owner selling the firm.
Alarmed in the 2028 world, where she expects to lose her job and turns first to **family and church**.
Her best long-term bet is **in-person work** with farmers, where trust counts.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, with small children, thin savings and slow learning.
whatWouldHelp: An **honest firm**, family support while she retrains, and her church close by.
